case_title: Union of India & Ors. v. Bodupalli Gopalaswami
accused_occupation: Army officer (Commandant of a Company ASC (Supply) supply depot)
statutory_provisions: Army Act, 1950 s.52(f) (charge 1); s.63 (charges 2 to 5); s.71 (punishment); Pension Regulation 16(a)
evidence_type: Witness testimony (13 prosecution witnesses), documentary evidence, material objects, and the inspection team's report
mitigating_circumstances: Limited overall-controlling role; charges technical in nature; subordinates held responsible for the lapses; matter over 20 years old and accused superannuated
trial_court_outcome: General Court Martial: guilty of charge 1, charge 4 and charge 5(c); not guilty of charges 2 and 3; sentenced to dismissal from service; pension forfeited later by President's order of 22.12.1995
high_court_outcome: Writ petition partly allowed: GCM proceedings, findings and dismissal upheld; order forfeiting pension quashed and reconsideration directed
offence_finally_established: Army Act s.52(f) (charge 1, intent to defraud, as a finding upheld); s.63 (charges 4 and 5(c), omissions prejudicial to good order and military discipline)
neutral_facts: The accused was the commanding officer of a military supply depot whose butchery supplied dressed meat, obtained from a private contractor, to indenting army units. The butchery was run by a supervisory officer, a veterinary officer, junior commissioned and non-commissioned officers, and the accused had overall charge of the depot. After complaints about irregularities, a team of three officers from a central investigating agency and two army officers carried out a surprise inspection of the butchery on 14 February 1990. The inspection team checked eleven vehicles returning from the butchery with meat. Of 1411.2 kg of dressed meat issued to various units, 14.5 kg was found to be heart, which was not an acceptable part of the carcass under the contract's special conditions. During discussions with the inspecting officers, the accused remarked that, to the best of the accused's knowledge, heart was an edible offal that could be issued on demand of units. The accused repeated this in a confidential report dated 15 February 1990. The prosecution case was that this remark amounted to accepting heart as part of the dressed meat with intent to defraud the government. There was no evidence that the accused had instructed heart to be accepted or that heart was regularly accepted. The supervisory and veterinary officers were separately charge-sheeted and punished. The prosecution also alleged that reserve stocks of animals were not maintained in the butchery between 11 and 22 March 1990, and that passed animals were not segregated from the contractor's other animals, contrary to the butchery's standard operating procedure.
offence_severity: Section 52(f): maximum ten years' imprisonment; Section 63: maximum seven years' imprisonment (minimum not stated)
number_of_offences: 5 charges (sections 52(f) and 63, i.e. 2 sections); 3 findings finally upheld (charges 1, 4 and 5(c))
motive: alleged: intent to defraud the government (charge 1); the Supreme Court found at best a wrong interpretation of clause 86
key_evidence_accepted: Inspection finding of 14.5 kg heart in 1411.2 kg of dressed meat; the accused's remark on heart as edible offal (as recorded); evidence that reserve shortfall and segregation lapses were largely the subordinates' or contractor's; Court did not disturb findings of guilt on charges 1, 4 and 5(c)
witness_credibility: Not assessed by the Supreme Court; it held that inadequacy and unreliability of evidence were not grounds for interference in judicial review
post_offence_conduct: Repeated the remark about heart in a confidential report dated 15.2.1990
trial_duration: offence: 14.2.1990 (inspection); trial judgment: 30.7.1993 (GCM sentence; trial commenced 22.1.1993); High Court: 25.8.2000; Supreme Court: 12.9.2011
legal_representation: Accused (respondent): Y. Rajagopala Rao, R. Balasubramanyam, Y. Ramesh, Sureshta Bagga. Union of India (appellants): P.P. Malhotra, ASG, with Rajiv Nanda, Rahul Kaushik, B.K. Prasad (for B.V. Balaram Das)
investigation_status: Surprise inspection (raid) conducted 14.2.1990; subordinate officials charge-sheeted and punished; charge-sheet against accused dated 30.12.1992; GCM convened and trial held
procedural_irregularity: None noted; plea that the Presiding Officer had earlier summarily tried two prosecution witnesses was rejected
appeal_history: Trial court (GCM): dismissal from service on 30.7.1993. High Court: writ partly allowed; pension forfeiture order quashed, proceedings and dismissal upheld. Supreme Court: Crl.A. 876/2003 (Union) allowed; Crl.A. 877/2003 (accused) allowed in part, dismissal substituted with forfeiture of eight years' service for pension and severe reprimand
prosecution_argument: Union of India contended that the High Court erred in quashing the order forfeiting pension, which was valid under Regulation 16(a) after dismissal
defence_argument: Presiding Officer was disqualified under Rule 39(2)(c) as he had summarily tried witnesses in the same incident and was biased, vitiating the GCM; the accused also contended that the punishment was disproportionate
legal_principle_applied: Judicial review of court martial is limited to lack of jurisdiction, excess of jurisdiction, or perverse or arbitrary action; punishment may be reviewed for proportionality only where shockingly disproportionate or perverse; Regulation 16(a) pension forfeiture is independent of s.71 punishment and falls if the dismissal is set aside
precedent_relied_upon: Union of India v. P.D. Yadav (2002) 1 SCC 405 (relied on); Union of India v. Major A. Hussain (1998) 1 SCC 537 (relied on); Ranjit Thakur v. Union of India (1987) 4 SCC 611 (relied on); Union of India v. R.K. Sharma (2001) 9 SCC 492 (referred to); Brig. A.K. Malhotra v. Union of India (1997) (4) SLR 51 (reversed in P.D. Yadav)
sentencing_rationale: Dismissal was shockingly disproportionate given the technical nature of the charges against the accused, the subordinates' responsibility and the contractor's breach; remand for a lesser punishment was not pursued because the matter was over 20 years old and the accused had superannuated; substituted punishment imposed
judicial_mitigating_factors: Technical and limited role of the accused; lapses attributable to subordinates and contractor; matter more than 20 years old; accused had superannuated
other_sentence_order: Pension order of 22.12.1995 set aside; pension claim to be processed and settled within six months; no back wages from dismissal to superannuation
